Semple|Semple]] | Virgulus | Raf. | Xalkitis | Raf. }} }} '''''Symphyotrichum''''' ({{IPAc-en|,|s|I|m|f|aI|@|'|t|r|I|k|@m}}) is a [[genus]] of over 100 species and naturally occurring hybrids of [[herbaceous]] [[annual plant|annual]] and [[perennial]] plants in the composite family, [[Asteraceae]], most which were formerly treated within the genus ''[[Aster (genus)|Aster]]''. The majority are [[endemic]] to [[North America]], but several also occur in the [[West Indies]], [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]], as well as one species in eastern [[Eurasia]]. Several species have been introduced to Europe as garden specimens, most notably New England aster (''[[Symphyotrichum novae-angliae]]'') and New York aster (''[[Symphyotrichum novi-belgii]]'').{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}}{{sfn|Everitt|Lonard|Little|2007}} ==Description== [[Luc Brouillet|Brouillet]], et al. wrote:
Taxonomy of ''Symphyotrichum'' is difficult. Species are usually [[wikt:heterophyllous|heterophyllous]], some strongly so. Individuals in the spring, with basal rosettes, often have leaf shapes quite different from those with [[cauline]] leaves seen later in the season. [[Phyllary]] shape on first- and later-formed [[flower heads|heads]] may differ. Individuals may vary considerably in plant size and array development depending upon growing conditions. The genetic diversity within each species also appears considerable.{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}}
For all species in the genus, the [[ray floret]]s are white, pink, blue, or purple. [[Disc floret]]s are yellow to white, becoming pinkish, reddish purple, or brown when mature. There are 5 lobes on the disc florets of all species in the genus.{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}} ==Taxonomy== German botanist [[Christian Gottfried Daniel Nees von Esenbeck]] established this genus in 1833 because he thought that a plant he examined, now believed to be a cultivated variety of New York aster (''[[Symphyotrichum novi-belgii]]''), which he called ''Symphyotrichum unctuosum'', was sufficiently distinct from the rest of the genus ''[[Aster (genus)|Aster]]'' to warrant its own genus. Nees emphasized the uniqueness of this plant in having its [[Pappus (flower structure)|pappus]] hairs arranged in a coherent, basal ring.{{sfn|Nees|1833}} This structure is likely the basis for the scientific name of this genus, which derives from the Greek [[wikt:συμφύω|συμφύω]] (''sumphúō''), meaning "unite", and [[wikt:θρίξ#Ancient_Greek|θρίξ, τριχός]] (''thríx'', ''trikhós''), meaning "hair".{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}} However, this characteristic ring is not generally shared by most New York aster pappi, nor is it characteristic of any other plants included in the modern concept of ''Symphyotrichum''. Regardless, according to the rules of the [[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants]] (ICN), the timing of the genus' establishment gives it precedence over other names. The genus was resurrected in 1994 by American botanist [[Guy L. Nesom]] to group together species formerly included in the genus ''Aster'' in order to make modern genera [[monophyletic]].{{sfn|Nesom|1994}} ===Subdivisions=== ''Symphyotrichum'' has been divided into five [[subgenera]]: ====Subgenus ''Ascendentes''==== This subgenus includes two species from the western United States and Canada that originated as hybrids between species in the subgenera ''Symphyotrichum'' and ''Virgulus''.{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}}{{sfn|Semple|n.d.a}} ====Subgenus ''Astropolium''==== This subgenus includes about 10 species found across the Americas in [[salt marsh]]es and [[salt pan (geology)|salt flats]].{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}}{{sfn|Semple|n.d.b}} ====Subgenus ''Chapmaniana''==== This subgenus includes a single species, ''[[Symphyotrichum chapmanii|S. chapmanii]]'', found in [[Alabama]] and [[Florida, Georgia & likely TN]].{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}} ====Subgenus ''Symphyotrichum''==== This subgenus includes about 65 species occurring across North America, including a few species in Central America and the Caribbean, with one species also occurring in Eurasia.{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}} ====Subgenus ''Virgulus''==== This subgenus includes about 28 species occurring across North America, including a few species in Central America and the Caribbean.{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}} ==Distribution== As a whole, ''Symphyotrichum'' is native throughout the Americas, with one species, ''[[Symphyotrichum ciliatum|S. ciliatum]]'', also native to eastern [[Eurasia]]. Several species have been introduced to Europe and other parts of the world.{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}} Most species are native to Mexico, the United States, and Canada, with several species occurring in the [[West Indies]] and [[Central America]].{{sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}}{{sfn|Gann|2021}}{{sfn|Britton|1914}}{{sfn|POWO|2021b}} Most members of subgenus ''Astropolium'' are restricted to South America.{{sfn|Semple|n.d.b}}{{sfn|Hind|Strange|2019}} ==Species== {{Main|List of Symphyotrichum species|l1=List of ''Symphyotrichum'' species}} {{As of|2021|June}}, [[Catalogue of Life]] listed 106 accepted species and identified naturally occurring hybrids, including the following:{{sfn|Hassler|2021}} * ''[[Symphyotrichum ascendens]]'' (Lindl.) G.L.Nesom – eastern annual saltmarsh aster == Reproduction == {{Multiple image | total_width = 320 | width = 160 | background color = #B4FAB4 | image1 = Asteraceae flower parts ray floret.svg | alt1 = refer to caption and text | caption1 = {{Center|Diagram of ray floret}} {{Ordered list | list_style_type = decimal | corolla | style | stigma | calyx | ovary }} | image2 = Asteraceae flower parts disk floret.svg | alt2 = refer to caption and text | caption2 = {{Center|Diagram of disk floret}} {{Ordered list | list_style_type = decimal | stigma | style | anthers | corolla | calyx | ovary }} }} Ray florets in the ''Symphyotrichum'' genus are exclusively female, each having a [[pistil]] (with [[Style (botany)|style]], [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]], and [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]]) but no [[stamen]]. Ray florets accept [[pollen]] and each can develop a [[seed]], but they produce no pollen.{{Sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}} Each ray floret has a strap-shaped corolla (or ligule) formed from three vestigial [[petal]]s which are fused together. The floret contains one inferior ovary, and this ovary contains one [[ovule]].{{efn|group=n|Asteraceae ovaries are called ''[[Inferior ovary|inferior]]'' because the floral parts attach above the ovary. See also ''[[Asteraceae#Floral structures|Asteraceae § Floral structures]]'' and ''[[Gynoecium]]''.}} The ovary has an attached style that extends outward from between the ray floret corolla and the rest of the flower head. As the ray floret is blooming, the stigma at the top of the style splits into two lobes.{{Sfn|Morhardt|Morhardt|2004|pp=30–31}} Disk florets in the ''Symphyotrichum'' genus are [[Hermaphrodite (botany)|androgynous]], each with both male (stamen, [[anther]]s, and [[Filament (botany)|filaments]]) and female reproductive parts; thus, a disk floret produces pollen and can develop a seed. The disk floret has five petals, sometimes referred to as ''lobes'', which are fused into its own corolla in the shape of a tube.{{Sfn|Brouillet|Semple|Allen|Chambers|2006}} The male stamen is inside the tube-shaped corolla of the disk floret. It has five anthers, five filaments, and produces pollen. The anthers and filaments are readily visible as separate entities in non-Asteraceae species. Here, they are fused together to form a cylinder, or tube, with their pollen on the inside only. This male anther cylinder surrounds the female style and stigma. As the style is maturing, it elongates up through the anther cylinder, gathering the pollen on its stigma along the way.{{Sfn|Morhardt|Morhardt|2004|p=30}} The ovary is at the bottom of the disk floret style. As with the ray floret, the disk floret stigma has two lobes that are fused together. The disk floret's stigma stays closed while pollen is on it, keeping its ovary safe from self-pollination. After the pollen has been collected and carried off by one or more pollinators, the stigma begins to split into two lobes, opening the style so that the disk floret ovary becomes accessible to receive pollen from another plant.{{Sfn|Morhardt|Morhardt|2004|p=30}} == Notes == {{Notelist|group=n}} == Citations == {{Reflist|20em}} == References == {{Refbegin|30em}} *{{Cite journal | last1 = Britton | first1 = N.L. | author-link1 = Nathaniel Lord Britton | date = January 1914 | title = Studies of West Indian Plants-V | url = https://www.jstor.org/stable/2479432 | journal = [[Journal of the Torrey Botanical Society|Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club]] | volume = 41 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–24 | doi = 10.2307/2479432 | doi-access = | jstor = 2479432 | language = en | access-date = 27 January 2021 | url-access= subscription }} *{{Cite eFloras | 1 | 132022 | Symphyotrichum | volume = 20 | date = 2006 | last1 = Brouillet | first1 = L. | author-link1 = Luc Brouillet | last2 = Semple | first2 = J.C. | author-link2 = John Cameron Semple | last3 = Allen | first3 = G.A. | author-link3 = Geraldine A.
